Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results demonstrate the TV-PARX model's effectiveness in forecasting counts and its ability to capture meaningful dynamics, as well as providing actionable insights for practitioners. From these findings, we conclude that the TV-PARX model offers a powerful tool for analyzing and predicting count-based time series data, surpassing the performance of established dynamic models, including the time-varying vector autoregressive model and the duration-dependent model. Moreover, the model's flexibility allows for the incorporation of external covariates, enabling the representation of complex relationships within such data sets. As a result, the TV-PARX model proves particularly suitable for analyzing and forecasting count-based time series data, offering a compelling alternative to established models.

This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. One such option is employing existing description systems themselves for evaluation purposes, which might be imperfect but could provide a more accurate assessment than completely random descriptions. Furthermore, we can utilize previously developed evaluation metrics such as BLEU, ROG, and METEOR, which compare system outputs to the available reference data, although with decreased accuracy. Additionally, we can also utilize other evaluation methods like human studies, although these are costly and time-consuming. Therefore, I propose the following evaluation protocol: Systems that produce more accurate descriptions in terms of metrics like BLEU, ROG, and METEOR are better suited to the task at hand. If a description system outperforms others based on these metrics on a given image set, it also likely produces more accurate descriptions for those images. Although not definitive, higher metric scores indicate a greater probability of the system describing images more accurately. On the other hand, if multiple systems have similar scores based on these metrics, further human evaluation is required to determine the best option. This proposed evaluation framework is particularly useful for the two proposed tasks: describing daily life images and providing verbal captions for videos. I believe this approach is more effective than the current method of solely relying on human-generated descriptions, which are subject to variability and bias, as demonstrated in Section 2. This proposed evaluation protocol also provides clearer directions for future description system development, which should lead to more accurate image description systems, as well as better description quality for both daily life images and video captions, which in turn benefits visually impaired individuals. Furthermore, this proposed framework should also be beneficial for other similar description systems, which could be applied to various tasks such as describing daily life images, providing verbal captions for videos, and translating text from one language to another, which should lead to a more substantial advancement in the field of computer vision.

the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the representation of noisy and missing information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on both text and multimedia content, outperforming the state-of-the-art techniques. The code and models of the system have been made available for download to facilitate future research.
